conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here.  
I’m Claire, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers sort through the emotional ups and downs that can come after a baby arrives. Over the next few minutes we’ll use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS for short). It’s simply a 10-item screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and mentally over the past seven days. Everything you share is confidential, and you can answer honestly without judgment—my goal is simply to listen and to make sure you have the support you need. When we finish, we’ll talk through what the results mean and any next steps that might help you feel more like yourself again.

We’ll go question by question; you can answer in your own words and I’ll jot down the score. Ready to start?

Here’s the first one:  
Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—maybe with your partner, friends, or even during those little moments with your baby?

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh. The other day my husband made a silly face while he was holding the baby and I couldn’t help giggling. It wasn’t quite the same belly-laugh I used to have, but I definitely still find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, that’s me—I’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yes, I still look forward to things. Like, I’m excited for our little weekend walk to the park tomorrow—just getting out with the baby and grabbing a coffee on the way. It feels nice to have something to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I really haven’t been doing that. If the baby spits up right after I’ve changed her, or if I’m running late because she needs an extra feed, I just figure it’s part of the new-mom learning curve. I don’t waste time beating myself up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I wouldn’t say I’m anxious “for no good reason.” I do get little flashes of worry—like when the baby’s breathing seems shallow or I wonder if she’s eating enough—but it feels pretty normal new-mom stuff, not this constant cloud of dread.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that way. No panic or sudden fear out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Not really—most days I feel like I’m staying on top of things. There are moments when the dishes pile up or the laundry feels endless, but I tackle them bit by bit and everything still feels manageable.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, nothing like that. I’ve been sleeping pretty well—when the baby gives me a decent stretch, I drift off easily and wake up rested. My mood hasn’t interfered with sleep at all.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt sad or miserable. Overall I’ve been pretty steady—tired sometimes, sure, but not down or weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried at all this week. I feel calm and okay; no tears or crying spells.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind. I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

You sound like you're adjusting to new motherhood with steady spirits. You still laugh with your partner, look forward to simple outings, and shrug off the small hiccups of baby care. Only occasional, baby-related worries flicker by, and you quickly resettle.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 1, Risk Level: Depression not likely
**Reasoning:** Lowest possible EPDS total of 1 reflects minimal distress. No <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym>, <sym>panic</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption from mood</sym>, <sym>crying</sym>, or <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym> reported. Worries are context-specific to infant well-being, not pervasive <med>generalized anxiety</med>. Score far below the 9-point threshold for possible <med>postpartum depression</med> and does not meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine well-baby and postpartum visits; re-screen if mood or functioning changes
2. Keep engaging in enjoyable daily activities and accept help with chores to sustain positive momentum
3. Practice brief breathing exercises when situational worries surface
4. Share any future mood, anxiety, or coping concerns promptly with your <med>OB provider</med> or <med>primary care clinician</med>
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 1: Postpartum Depression Screening – EPDS-10 (informal)

Symptoms endorsed  
- No sustained low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia, or self-blame  
- Occasional situational worries about infant health (not pervasive)  
- Denies sleep disturbance from mood, panic, or self-harm ideation  

Pattern  
Consistently positive affect, preserved enjoyment, and adequate coping; no indicators of depression or anxiety above “normal new-parent concerns.”

Screening significance  
Current responses place total score at the lowest possible range; no red flags for major postpartum depression or anxiety. Continue routine psychosocial monitoring at pediatric/OB visits; re-screen if clinical picture changes.
